attributes.body:
いらっしゃる is another of the common honorific language expressions in Japanese. This means that it elevates the status of another person, in order to pay them respect. It will never be used when referring to the speaker themselves, or their own actions.

いらっしゃる can be used to replace 居（い）る 'to be', 来（く）る 'to come', or 行（い）く 'to go'. This is due to the unique perspective that honorific language places the speaker in, in relation to the person that is being respected. This is a slightly advanced concept that we will discuss more later.

To use いらっしゃる, simply replace いる, くる, or いく with いらっしゃる.

Alternatively, いらっしゃる may also be used to replace いる, くる, or いく when they are attached to the て-form of another verb.

Fun Fact

おいでになる is another expression which can replace いる, くる, or いく. This was briefly examined previously in our お～になる grammar point. おいでになる and いらっしゃる are almost completely interchangable.

These are honorific forms used to respectfully describe others' actions. お～になる is used with regular verbs, e.g. 書く 'write' becoming お書きになる (same meaning, but showing respect to the writer). いらっしゃる is a special honorific form that replaces 行く, 来る, and いる, for which the お～になる form is not used.

second_relatable.title: いらっしゃる
second_relatable.meaning: To be (Honorific), To come (Honorific), To go (Honorific)

attributes.body: がいる combines the particle が with the verb いる to express the existence of living or animate beings, like people or animals. いらっしゃる is the honorific equivalent of いる, as well as 行く and 来る. In other words, がいらっしゃる is the honorific version of がいる, and いらっしゃいますか is the honorific equivalent of いますか, 行きますか, or 来ますか.

attributes.body: Both いらっしゃる and くる express movement toward the speaker, similar to the English 'come.' The key difference is politeness: くる is the neutral verb used in everyday contexts, while いらっしゃる is an honorific verb used to show respect for someone's movement. Note that いらっしゃる also serves as the honorific form of いる, いく, and くる.

attributes.body: Both いらっしゃる and いく express movement away from the speaker, similar to the English 'go.' The key difference is politeness: いく is a neutral verb used in everyday contexts, while いらっしゃる is a polite, honorific verb used to show respect for someone's movement. Note that いらっしゃる also serves as the honorific form of いる, くる, and いく.
